cim: Artificial intelligence at UC, the modern-day flame of Prometheus
cim_eredeti: Artificial intelligence at UC, the modern-day flame of Prometheus
szoveg_eredeti:
Carl H. Lindner Hall at the University of Cincinnati on Nov. 4, 2026.

According to ancient Greek myth, humans first encountered fire when the titan Prometheus snuck into the workshop of Hephaestus, god of blacksmiths, and stole a spark of divine flame in a hollowed-out fennel stalk. This spark was a gift to the mortals punished by Zeus to suffer cold, hungry and weak lives as a result of Prometheus’s trickery.

The rogue immortal presented humanity with an unfamiliar technology with unknown possibilities. Today, artificial intelligence (AI) is like a modern-day version of that flame, according to Kris Jones, academic director of the Master of Science in information systems at the University of Cincinnati.

AI, Jones says, is a sort of Promethean technology. “So, I always like to say, ‘I like to use fire to heat my house, to keep warm, cook a great meal,’ and so forth,” Jones said. “But if I'm not using it correctly, I can burn down my house. I can burn down my neighbor's house, right?”

This idea of safe and responsible use seems to be the guiding principle for UC departments that are cautiously incorporating AI into their work and curriculum. This article will examine how four of them — Digital Technology Solutions, the Center for the Enhancement of Teaching and Learning, Electrical and Computer Engineering and Information Systems — are using AI.

Digital Technology Solutions (DTS) is UC’s central IT service provider. This department not only provides IT help when a system doesn’t work the way it’s supposed to, but it also develops new technologies designed to help students and faculty. One such new technology is BearcatGPT, UC’s private, secure, generative AI platform that is accessible to current students, staff and faculty.

The platform, piloted in December 2025 and made available to students in the spring of 2026, interfaces with UC systems and offers a more secure form of the GenAI experience, according to Josette Riep, associate vice president and chief data & AI officer of DTS.

“BearcatGPT is the university's private multi-LLM environment,” Riep said. The multi-LLM she refers to stands for large language models, systems that can process multiple types of data. “And so basically, it's an environment that's within UC's network. We're not sharing data, you know, with large language models outside of UC. We're not educating them with your information.”

Riep says that the purpose of BearcatGPT is to be both safe and empowering for people in UC to use.

“So, there's definitely a big pickup in terms of your STEM classes, so you know, all of your math and stats classes,” Riep said. “There's definitely a lot of traction there. There's a lot of traction in chemistry, physics. However, there's also CCM, you know, who's using it for different purposes. And so, it's really diverse, I think.”

While DTS is making advances into AI on campus, the Center for the Enhancement of Teaching and Learning (CET&L) helps instructors learn how to incorporate technology directly into their classes.

Assistant Director Daniel Dale says that in terms of AI, CET&L usually helps professors in one of two areas: resistance or integration.

“So that could be figuring out like, ‘How do I think AI is going to be used in my discipline? How can I help students gain the skills necessary to prepare them for their future career or for the fields that they're going into?’” Dale said. “Or sometimes instructors are like, ‘I don't really feel like AI really helps students reach the learning outcomes in my course, so I'm interested in designing a course that kind of is AI resistant or encourages students to avoid using AI.’”

For faculty who want to make their classes more resistant, Dale talks with them about how certain assignments can invite more AI use than others. Dale says he helps faculty identify “low hanging fruit” in their courses, like short quizzes and reading summaries, while still creating assignments that meet the same learning goals and encourage students to use their own minds to figure it out.

In terms of AI integration, Dale says that AI should be tailored to the discipline in question. “It's more about like thinking about ‘Well, I'm going to be using AI in these ways when I'm outside the class,’” Dale said. “‘How can I, as an instructor, create learning experiences that simulate what these students will be doing outside the course inside the course?’”

UC’s department of Electrical and Computer Engineering (ECE) is actively trying to embrace and educate about AI. For example, Medhi Norouzi created and teaches two graduate level courses called Applied Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning and Applied Generative AI: A Deep Learning Approach Across Modalities.

Department Head Marc Cahay often encourages his research students to use AI to gather literature related to their research. He notes that these sources should still be looked at by students to determine relevance and validity but adds that if there is an engine to streamline the process, then it should be used.

Additionally, thanks to funding from the Ohio Cyber Range Institute, ECE will soon start researching and exploring connections between AI and cyber security, looking at how to make open-source AI platforms more secure to protect what people put in them.

Lastly, ECE is using AI to help make classes more ADA compliant, speeding up the process and making it more efficient. Cahay said that, for example, AI tools can take handwritten notes, gesturing to the ones all over his desk and walls, and turn them into a more accessible audio or PowerPoint presentations. As someone with a Belgian accent, he says this tool has helped him overcome that barrier.

“There are tools which will scan this, put [it] in a form which is readable, and then it takes this and puts in the PowerPoint, and then it takes that and puts it in an audio for that PowerPoint, because obviously I have an accent,” Cahay said. “So, when you put in an audio, it will be a nice voice of a lady talking and making the conversation.”

Academic Director Kris Jones, who teaches a number of information systems courses at Lindner, says there is a duality to AI. It’s more about how the technology is being used that determines whether it can help or harm, according to Jones.

“As I brought it into the classroom, I'm thinking about ‘How do I motivate students to wield this technology for good?’” Jones said. “Not just to be harvesting knowledge and so forth, but actually doing authentic learning.”

Jones uses AI to help design different engagement activities for his students. Using the example of business intelligence, he details how he uses AI to create different scenarios in which someone might have to use business intelligence and how it can be used right now as a student.

Jones says that a major reason students use AI is because they don’t feel motivated by their class work or don’t feel it is relevant to their career goals, so they use it to avoid spending time on work they believe is tedious. So, instead of only having students do typical assignments like research papers, Jones creates assignments where students use AI as a copilot.

“Yes, I still do projects,” Jones said. “You have to still practice. I still do tests and everything like that, too. But I think that's for a good repetition and memorization. But when we get to that applied side, that's where it's got to be hands on. And right now, why not use AI to help you create hands-on activities that could really be a lot more personalized to my class versus it just being something that I got out of a textbook?”

By developing private and secure AI serves, creating more interactive and specialized assignments and using AI to make classes more accessible, these departments have grazed the surface of AI’s capabilities. As AI research, development and exploration at UC persists, what began as a small spark will likely continue to grow into a powerful flame.
